take.head: Bengals edge Huntley's Ravens in a low one
take.lean:
Tyler Huntley has to throw his way past a Bengals pass defense that ranks 8th, and in Cleveland he managed 165 yards. Lamar Jackson misses a third straight game. That gap is huge: Jackson's passes were among the league's most productive, while Huntley's barely help the offense at all. Baltimore scored 10 points last week, and the passer is the reason.

So the Ravens lean on Derrick Henry, which is harder than it sounds. Henry ran for 58 yards on 17 carries in Cleveland and lost a late fumble that set up the tying touchdown. Cincinnati ranks 8th against backs. Henry's workload is safe because he takes about three of every four carries and a close game keeps him on the field. But the yards come slowly, and he lands right around his projection instead of bouncing back big.

When the run game stalls, Huntley runs. He took 21.7 percent of Baltimore's carries last week, and Cincinnati ranks 18th against quarterbacks. His scrambles and short scores push his fantasy day past his projection even while the offense sputters.

Zay Flowers is the passing game. Last week he drew 35.5 percent of the targets, and that volume holds. Against a defense that ranks 9th against receivers, though, it turns into catches like his six for 66 in Cleveland: useful in half-PPR, not a ceiling game. The softer spot is Mark Andrews. Cincinnati ranks 22nd against tight ends, and a passer who works short and over the middle finds him more than the last two weeks suggest.

The other side is where the game is won, but not easily. Joe Burrow comes off the bye with nobody on the injury report, and he leads the league in completion rate at 71.4 percent. Baltimore's defense ranks 6th against quarterbacks, though, and it sacks passers often enough to stall drives. Burrow wins the game without the big day his projection asks for.

He wins it outside. Baltimore ranks 20th against receivers, the one real crack in that defense, and Ja'Marr Chase drew 32.3 percent of the targets in his last full game. Chase gets the matchup and the volume and clears his projection. Tee Higgins plays the same weak secondary, but his share swings too much week to week to trust beyond his number.

On the ground, Cincinnati has nothing to work with. The Bengals' run game is below average, Baltimore ranks 6th against backs, and Samaje Perine took 45.2 percent of the carries in week 5. That leaves Chase Brown short.

All of that keeps both teams out of the high 20s. Cincinnati's defense allows touchdowns on 41.2 percent of red-zone trips, so Baltimore's drives that do get close end in field goals. The Bengals pull ahead late through Chase, but a Ravens defense this good keeps it inside the number.

take.head: Watson throws Browns past a thin Titans offense
take.lean:
Deshaun Watson gets to throw against a Titans pass defense that ranks 27th, and neither offense has a bigger edge than that. Cleveland has one of the league's worst run games. It knows that, and it throws more than most teams when the game is close. Watson has been about a league-average passer this year. Against this secondary, average is enough to move the ball.

Those drives stall short of the end zone, though. Cleveland gives up sacks more often than almost anyone, and Tennessee's rush gets home. So Watson finishes drives with field goals, the same way he has for weeks: 16 of 26 for 164 yards and no touchdowns in last week's win over Baltimore. He has missed his projection three straight weeks, and a high fantasy projection doesn't fit an offense that scores 17.7 a game.

The yards go to Denzel Boston. He plays nearly every snap and gets a steady fifth of the targets, and the Titans rank 23rd against receivers. KC Concepcion and Jerry Jeudy split what's left. Harold Fannin Jr. has caught almost nothing for two weeks, and Tennessee ranks 8th against tight ends, so that slump keeps going.

Quinshon Judkins is healthy and faces a run defense that is about league average. The Browns' line is the problem, not the matchup. His catches out of the backfield keep him near his projection, and with Dylan Sampson active, he gives up a few touches.

On the other side, Cam Ward has nobody to throw to. Calvin Ridley and Tyjae Spears are both out, and the Titans scored 14 a game even with them. Denzel Ward plays through his hand injury and lines up across from Carnell Tate. Tate is Tennessee's only receiver who wins outside, and Cleveland's pass defense ranks 9th. Tate's touchdown in the Colts game was real, but against Ward it's a fight for every catch.

With Tate covered, the short throws go to Wan'Dale Robinson. He drew seven targets last week and turned them into 22 yards. The volume is solid and climbs again here. Expect more catches and more yards from the same role. Ward the quarterback has scored 5.0 and 6.8 the last two weeks and gets no easier matchup.

Without Spears, Tony Pollard has the backfield to himself, including passing downs. He took 82.6 percent of the carries last week. But the Browns allow the second-fewest points to backs, so the extra touches keep him at his projection rather than above it.

Neither offense runs many plays, so there aren't many possessions to go around. Cleveland's field goals come from the one matchup it wins every week. Tennessee's two missing playmakers leave it chasing late against a defense that has held every opponent in check.
take.vs: Agree it's low scoring. I have the Browns a point above their 19 because Watson's passing beats this secondary, and the Titans below 17.5 without Ridley and Spears.

take.head: Vikings defense swallows a turnover-prone Colts
take.lean:
Kyler Murray finally has his whole receiving group back, and he gets it against a Colts secondary missing Sauce Gardner. Jordan Addison and T.J. Hockenson both practiced fully. Slot corner Justin Walley is questionable with a bad knee, so Indianapolis may line up backups at two of its three corner spots against Justin Jefferson.

The Vikings' offense has a real flaw. Murray takes sacks far too often, and the offense rarely gains enough on a play to stay on schedule. The Colts can't exploit it. Their pass rush barely gets home, and Arden Key, their best edge rusher, is on IR. Murray should get clean pockets, and Jefferson is the main beneficiary against a pass defense that ranks 20th. Addison and Hockenson take the middle of the field, which keeps Indianapolis from doubling Jefferson.

Minnesota's run game is one of the league's worst, and Jordan Mason's return off IR makes it harder to trust. He and Aaron Jones will split the work. The Colts allow plenty to backs, but neither Viking back gets enough touches to cash in.

Daniel Jones has the harder job. Minnesota's defense allows 12.8 points a game and gives up the fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks and to backs. Jones ranks near the bottom of the league in completion rate. The Colts have 11 giveaways, and Tyler Warren is out, a tight end who played 91 percent of the snaps. Without him, Keenan Allen becomes the short-area target Jones leans on. That keeps Allen's floor steady, but Josh Downs gets squeezed.

The Colts want to win through Jonathan Taylor. He's their best player, but he faces the defense that allows the fewest points to backs, and he lost a fumble last week. Once Minnesota leads by two scores, Indianapolis has to throw into a pass rush that hits the quarterback constantly. That's how the extra turnovers come, and how the Vikings pull away late. Minnesota's offense is good enough to win, not to run up the score, so the game stays low.
take.vs: I agree on the shape: a Vikings win in a low-scoring game. Minnesota pulls a little further ahead because the Colts' rush can't punish Murray's sack habit and the Colts keep giving the ball away.
take.risk: Taylor breaks long runs and Jones protects the ball, or Minnesota keeps stalling in the red zone and settles for field goals.

take.head: Smith's clean pocket sinks Miami
take.lean:
Geno Smith gets a clean pocket against a Miami defense that almost never reaches the quarterback. The Dolphins have sacked passers on 2.5% of pass plays, and only one defense in the league gives up more on each throw. That helps this Jets team more than most. Their line has struggled to keep Smith upright, and their run game is one of the league's weakest. With the pass rush gone, the one thing New York does well has room to work.

The production goes somewhere you wouldn't expect. Miami ranks 2nd against wide receivers but 29th against tight ends and 30th against backs. Teams beat this defense underneath and over the middle, not outside. That makes Mason Taylor the sneaky play: he drew a fifth of the targets last week and lines up right where Miami breaks down. It also keeps Garrett Wilson near his usual output rather than the big day the matchup seems to promise. Omar Cooper broke out while Adonai Mitchell was out. Mitchell is cleared and back, so Cooper's share shrinks.

Breece Hall sits with the quad, so Braelon Allen carries the backfield again on 87% of the snaps. He won't break many long runs. He doesn't need to: steady carries against a defense that gives up points to backs, plus Smith's checkdowns, push him past his projection. Isaiah Davis stays a change-of-pace back with a handful of touches.

Miami can't keep up with that kind of steady offense. Under Malik Willis the Dolphins score 14 points a game, and Willis has 4 interceptions and 5 fumbles in five starts. His right thumb was enough of a worry to make the injury report, even after a full week of practice. The Jets lost Joseph Ossai and David Onyemata up front, which weakens their pass rush. Willis gives the ball away without pressure anyway, and every short field he hands the Jets is a drive Miami can't afford.

Ollie Gordon II is the Miami player to trust. He has taken about half the carries with De'Von Achane on injured reserve and beat his projection in both games. The Jets rank 22nd against backs, and Miami will lean on him to stay out of long passing downs. Malik Washington draws close to a third of the targets, enough to land near his projection even with weak throws coming his way. Greg Dulcich runs into a Jets defense that ranks 5th against tight ends.

One roster note: Tyreek Hill is not on Miami. He is a free agent rehabbing his knee, so he belongs nowhere near a lineup. The Jets pull away after halftime on Smith's arm and Allen's carries while Miami keeps handing the ball back.
take.vs: Disagree on Miami: 18 points is more than an offense scoring 14 a game has earned. The Jets land near their 21.5 because Miami barely sacks Smith.
take.risk: If Willis protects the ball and his scrambles extend drives, Gordon keeps Miami within a field goal and the weak Jets run game can't close it out.

take.head: Texans win, but Giants stay inside the number
take.lean:
Stroud gets time to throw against a Giants pass rush that rarely reaches the quarterback. The Giants are without Burns and Golston up front and Newsome at corner. Houston's passing has been well above average this season, and Stroud has beaten his projection three weeks in a row. He keeps that going here.

The Houston receiver to own is Noel. He has beaten his projection three straight weeks while Collins's share of the targets has shrunk. The Giants rank 16th against receivers, so neither man faces a wall, but Noel is getting the open looks right now. Collins still gets his catches, just not the big game his name suggests. Schultz has slipped into a part-time role.

Houston can't run the ball. Its ground game is one of the league's worst, and with Montgomery's groin keeping him out, the backfield belongs to Marks, with only Ogunbowale behind him. Marks gets the volume against a Giants defense that ranks 21st against backs. But volume in a bad run game leaves him near his projection, not past it. It also means Houston can't burn the clock once it gets ahead.

That gives the Giants their opening. Harbaugh starts McCarthy over the benched Winston, and Houston plays without both of its safeties, Pitre and Blankenship. The defense already ranks 28th against receivers, and now its last line is gone. Nabers has drawn more than a third of the targets in each of the last two weeks. Likely works the middle of the field, which is exactly where backup safeties get exposed. Both beat their projections.

McCarthy cuts both ways. He runs more than Winston did and adds points with his legs, but he has 13 career interceptions to go with 12 touchdowns. Houston's pass rush also gets home far more often than the Giants' does. Expect one turnover that hands Houston a short field. Expect McCarthy to answer with a couple of long drives built on Nabers. He lands near his projection.

The Giants won't run their way back into it. Skattebo returns from a six-snap week into a split with Tracy, against a Houston defense that ranks 10th against backs. Tracy keeps third downs, Skattebo takes early downs, and neither gets enough to matter. The Giants throw because they have to, and Nabers and Likely pile up catches late.

Stroud's arm wins it for Houston. Without a run game to close it out or its safeties to hold the back end, though, Houston doesn't pull away. Both teams score, and the Giants are still within one score at the end.

take.head: Purdy's 49ers outlast Penix in Atlanta
take.lean:
Purdy throws from a clean pocket, and that matters more than who catches the ball. His line has allowed a sack on 2.6% of his pass plays. With Evans and Samuel out, the passing game runs through McCaffrey and Kittle, while Kirk debuts next to Cooks and Watkins.

Atlanta has no answer for that pair. Its pass defense sits in the middle of the league, and it ranks 24th against tight ends. That makes Kittle the first read on every pass play. Last week McCaffrey caught nine of 10 targets in the same short role, and Atlanta's run defense alone will not stop him.

Penix has the opposite problem. When he is kept clean he is one of the league's better passers. Under quick pressure he has gone 3 of 15 for 17 yards, and Chicago sacked him five times last week. Bosa is out, but he played only two games. The San Francisco defense that allows 18.3 points a game has mostly played without him already.

That pushes Atlanta to Bijan Robinson, and with Brian Robinson out he gets nearly all the carries, with Herbert behind him. Volume keeps him useful, but this defense gives up big plays on only 4.5% of snaps. He has to grind out short gains, not break the long run that saves his week. His catches out of the backfield keep his floor intact.

San Francisco finishes drives and goes ahead, and Atlanta has to chase. That feeds London targets against a defense that ranks 10th against receivers, so he needs volume to reach his number. Pitts runs into a defense that ranks 4th against tight ends after two scores last week. Every long third down puts Penix back in the quick-pressure spots where he struggles.

Both offenses run fewer plays than the league average, and San Francisco is happy to burn the clock with McCaffrey once it leads. Atlanta stays within reach, but it never gets the ball back enough times to turn it around.

take.head: Young's arm outguns a limping Bucs passing game
take.lean:
Tampa's front stops the run, so Carolina wins this through the air: Bryce Young and Tetairoa McMillan against a Bucs secondary playing without safety Antoine Winfield Jr. Young is one of the league's best passers per play this year. Carolina has gone from 18.3 points a game last season to 29.2, and the passing game is the reason.

The Panthers have to go that way because Chuba Hubbard won't find room. Tampa allows backs 14.8 half-PPR points a game, fourth fewest in the league. Hubbard keeps nearly every carry, but this week those carries mostly set up passing downs. He finishes under his projection even with the work.

With Xavier Legette on injured reserve, Carolina's targets narrow to two receivers. Jalen Coker drew 13 targets last week. McMillan is the one who wins against Tampa's cornerbacks. Darren Waller has faded out of the offense and stays on benches.

Tampa can't keep up. Baker Mayfield returns from his thumb injury, but in his three games this year he was worse per pass than backup Jalon Daniels. Now he loses Emeka Egbuka and right tackle Luke Goedeke. Tampa already gets sacked on 9.1 percent of its pass plays. Carolina is missing edge Jaelan Phillips, which takes some heat off the line, but not enough to fix Mayfield's season.

Without Egbuka, Chris Godwin Jr. becomes the top target, but Carolina's defense is seventh against receivers, so his extra looks turn into short catches. More of the passing game runs through the middle to Cade Otton, against a defense that ranks 25th against tight ends.

Bucky Irving is the Bucs' way to stay in the game. Carolina gives up 23.3 points a game to backs, among the league's worst. Irving took 76 percent of the carries last week, so the job is his. Tampa leans on him to shorten the game and keep Young off the field. That keeps the score down, but it doesn't flip the result.

Carolina gets ahead in the first half, and Tampa has to throw from behind. That is when the Bucs fall apart: they have 11 giveaways in six games. The Panthers win by more than a field goal.

take.head: Nix rebounds, but Denver can't pull away

Arizona's pass defense ranks 30th, and it gets thinner here: Andrew Wingard and Walter Nolen III are out, Will Johnson is on IR, and Budda Baker and Max Melton are both questionable. Nix was good last year and has been bad this year. Last week he threw for 107 yards against Seattle. This is the week his numbers come back.

Waddle leads that rebound. His target share rose to 29.2 percent last week, and Arizona gives up the seventh-most points to receivers. He catches enough short throws to beat a modest projection. Sutton runs plenty of routes but has done little with them, so he stays a flex at best.

The ceiling comes from how slowly Denver plays. The Broncos run fewer plays than almost anyone and have scored 19.0 points a game. A cleaner day from Nix gets Denver to the low 20s, not to a blowout. Arizona's run defense is one of the league's better ones, so the Broncos' drives go through the air. That gives Dobbins a steady but capped day as the early-down back, while Harvey's work catching passes keeps him near his number.

Arizona's half of the game is harder. Denver's defense ranks 3rd against the pass, and Brissett has scored single digits in two of his last three games. Pat Surtain is reportedly unlikely to play, which helps Wilson some, but Denver still allows the eighth-fewest points to receivers. Wilson lands near his projection, not above it.

McBride still gets his targets, but he turns them into short, low-scoring catches. He went 7 catches for 53 yards last week, and this pass defense is tougher than the Rams'. Expect a busy line that falls short of his projection.

Arizona's points come on the ground. With Jeremiyah Love out, Bam Knight was the back who actually gained yards last week, 15 carries for 80 yards against Allgeier's 18 for 38. Denver gives up the ninth-most points to backs. Knight gets the bigger share of the work and outscores Allgeier.

That keeps Arizona in it. Denver's offense doesn't build big leads, and an Arizona run game led by Knight keeps the clock moving and the game within one score. Denver wins it, but with field goals more than touchdowns, and the Cardinals stay inside the number.

take.head: Gibbs runs Detroit past the Packers' thin front

Jahmyr Gibbs gets a Green Bay front that is missing Edgerrin Cooper and Javon Hargrave, and this is where Detroit wins. The Packers already ranked 31st against backs before their best linebacker and their interior tackle went to IR. Gibbs beats them on the ground and as a receiver, and every long Detroit drive takes a possession away from Jordan Love.

Green Bay can't answer on the ground. Its run game is close to the worst in the league, and Josh Jacobs returns from the Commissioner's Exempt List with only two practices behind him. He and MarShawn Lloyd, who ran eight times for 10 yards last week, split a light workload against a Lions defense that ranks 7th against backs. The Packers can't stay on schedule by running, so every drive falls on Love.

That is Green Bay's way to keep it close. No team gives quarterbacks more fantasy points than Detroit. The secondary is thin, with Avonte Maddox and Thomas Harper on IR and Rock Ya-Sin questionable. Love's back is fine after a full practice Thursday. Matthew Golden is the receiver to start: he drew a 32.5 percent target share last week. Tucker Kraft faces a defense that gives tight ends the most in football. Christian Watson is cleared, but Golden is the one getting the targets.

Detroit's passing game doesn't get the same gift. Jared Goff has 12 touchdowns and no picks, but Green Bay's pass defense ranks 7th and almost never gives up a big play. Goff works the short and middle routes. That keeps Amon-Ra St. Brown near his usual output and limits Jameson Williams' deep shots. Sam LaPorta's two big weeks end against a defense that ranks 6th against tight ends.

The result is a game Green Bay keeps within reach through the air but never controls. Detroit's run game is the one advantage that lasts all four quarters, and Gibbs is the reason the Lions win by more than a field goal.

take.head: Rams edge it, but the Raiders cover at home
take.lean:
Kirk Cousins gets clean pockets against a Rams front playing without Myles Garrett and Kobie Turner, both on IR. Los Angeles already reaches the quarterback far less often than it did last year. Las Vegas has kept Cousins upright all season, and he has carried a passing game that scores 27 points a game, even though the Raiders' run game is one of the league's worst.

Those clean pockets still throw into the toughest part of this Rams defense. Los Angeles allows the fewest points in the league to tight ends and ranks 4th against receivers. Brock Bowers sees too many targets to disappear, but this matchup holds him near his usual line. Tre Tucker's two-touchdown week against Buffalo was a spike, and he comes back down here. Ashton Jeanty runs behind that bad line into a Rams defense that ranks 12th against backs, so his catches are what keep him in lineups. The Raiders move the ball, but in steady drives rather than big plays.

The other side of the ball is where the Rams' trouble is. Davante Adams is out for 6-10 weeks, and Puka Nacua missed Friday's practice with a calf injury. The team calls the injury minor, and if he plays he gets fed. He drew a 44.4 percent target share in week 5. Beyond him, Matthew Stafford's receivers are Konata Mumpfield and Tutu Atwell. That is not enough to stretch a defense, and it is why the Rams' offense has fallen from 30.5 points a game last year to 22.5.

That sends Sean McVay to Kyren Williams, and Las Vegas is the right defense for it. The Raiders rank 27th against backs and give up touchdowns on 73.9 percent of opponents' red-zone trips, so Williams's goal-line carries turn into scores. Tyler Higbee picks up the short targets Adams leaves behind, against a defense that ranks 27th against tight ends. Stafford lands about where he usually does: efficient underneath, without many deep shots.

The Rams win because their backfield beats a soft Raiders run defense. The market has already moved off its opening number, but it still rates the version of this Rams offense that had Adams and a healthy Nacua. Without them, Los Angeles has to grind out every drive, and Cousins keeps Las Vegas within one score to the final whistle.
take.vs: Close to the implied score. LV lands near its 22.5, but LA's thin receiving room keeps it a point under 26. The Rams win by less than the spread.

take.head: Chiefs win the turnover battle in Seattle
take.lean:
Sam Darnold has thrown 7 interceptions in six games. This week he faces a Chiefs defense that ranks 4th against quarterbacks. Seattle has turned the ball over 12 times, and Kansas City has done it 3 times in five games. That gap decides this game.

Seattle can't run the ball to protect him. By how many points a play adds, the Seahawks have the league's worst run game. With Zach Charbonnet's knee keeping him out, Emanuel Wilson is the lead back, and he runs into a Kansas City defense that ranks 5th against backs. Wilson gets the carries but gains little with them. That leaves Darnold throwing on obvious passing downs. He was a different quarterback for this team in 2025. This year he keeps forcing throws, and Kansas City has 8 takeaways to show it can make him pay.

The Chiefs know where the ball is going. Jaxon Smith-Njigba drew 34.8% of Seattle's targets last week, and Kansas City gives up the fewest wide receiver points in the league. He still gets his catches because nobody else in this offense commands the ball. His big games come on deep throws, and this secondary doesn't allow those. The one opening is at tight end, where the Chiefs rank 28th. AJ Barner has been on the field for almost every snap and has done nothing with it. This matchup gives him his best chance at a useful line.

Kansas City's passing game faces the tougher test. Seattle ranks 2nd against the pass and allows the 2nd-fewest quarterback points. Rashee Rice is out, Tyquan Thornton is on IR and Jaylon Moore is out on the offensive line. Patrick Mahomes won't win this with his receivers. Xavier Worthy is his top target and gets volume at a 24.1% share, but every catch comes against a defense that allows the 3rd-fewest wide receiver points. Travis Kelce was limited Thursday with an ankle injury and draws a defense that gives tight ends the 3rd-fewest points.

That sends the Chiefs to Kenneth Walker III, who faces the team that let him go. Seattle ranks 17th against backs, the weakest part of a strong defense. Walker leads the NFL in rushing and ran for 128 yards and 2 touchdowns last week. Kansas City's run game adds points instead of losing them, and Walker gets most of its carries. He's the one player here with both the volume and the matchup.

There's a 51% chance of light rain at kickoff. Both teams already lean on defense, and the rain pushes them further toward short throws and handoffs. Points come slowly. In a low-scoring game, the team that gives Seattle short fields loses, and Darnold is the quarterback who gives them up.
take.vs: Disagree on the side. The market gives Seattle 22.8; Darnold's turnovers and a run game going nowhere hold Seattle under 20 against KC's 4th-ranked defense vs QBs.
take.risk: Darnold plays like he did in 2025 and protects the ball, or Seattle's pass rush beats a line missing Jaylon Moore and forces Mahomes into turnovers.

take.head: Dallas wins, McKee and Goedert keep it close
take.lean:
Tanner McKee gets the friendliest pass defense in football, and he gets it without DeVonta Smith or Dontayvion Wicks. Dallas ranks last in the league against the pass and rarely hits the quarterback. McKee will have clean pockets all night. What he lacks is someone to throw to.

That someone is Dallas Goedert. He practiced in full Saturday, and he drew roughly a quarter of the targets in week 5, when the receiver room was healthier. With Smith out, only Goedert and Makai Lemon have a real claim on volume. Darius Cooper caught one of two targets in the 25-14 loss to Carolina, and Marquise Brown sits third on the depth chart.

That sets Philadelphia's limit. Even with Jalen Hurts, this offense hardly produced a big play all season. McKee threw for 222 yards in his first start, but it took him 48 pass plays and the Eagles scored 14 points. This week the field is softer. Dallas gives up 26.5 points a game, and drives that died at midfield in Carolina reach field-goal range here. Philadelphia scores in the low 20s, not the teens.

Dallas still has the better offense, and Philadelphia's defense helps it. The Eagles' pass rush was already one of the league's quietest, and now it plays without Nolan Smith, with Jalyx Hunt questionable. Dak Prescott has fallen short in each of the last two weeks and threw two interceptions against Green Bay. This defense has 3 takeaways all season, though, so he can hold the ball and wait for CeeDee Lamb.

Lamb is the play of the game. He drew 18 targets against the Packers, and Philadelphia gives up the second-most fantasy points to receivers in the league. George Pickens practiced in full through his shoulder injury and gets the same thin secondary. Ryan Flournoy has become Prescott's third option and scored last week. Jake Ferguson is the one left out, and his share keeps shrinking.

On the ground, Javonte Williams owns Dallas's carries against a run defense in the middle of the league. That makes him steady, not a ceiling play. Philadelphia's backfield is the murkier spot. Saquon Barkley is expected back from a hamstring injury that cost him two games, but Dameon Pierce took 92.3 percent of the carries last week and scored. Barkley comes back to a shared backfield, and the split caps both of them.

Dallas moves the ball more reliably and leads most of the night. Its defense can't get Philadelphia off the field in the second half, though, and a home team throwing into the league's worst secondary keeps this a one-score game to the end. Start Lamb and Goedert with confidence. Barkley is a flex with a lower floor than his name suggests.
take.vs: Agree on Dallas near 24, but Philadelphia gets past 19.5. A defense allowing 26.5 a game lets even a backup-led offense finish drives.
take.risk: McKee turns the ball over like a backup, or Lamb's volume turns into multiple touchdowns, and Dallas pulls away by halftime.
